label: Color & clarity principles
_note: Editorial color-selection rules grounded in the cited fish-vision science (T3). Each `rule` is a synthesis and labelled editorial; the `citations` are verbatim quotes. Meant to be calibrated against the logbook over time.

principles.label: Depth absorbs red first
principles.rule: At depth, red/orange are absorbed first — reds read as grey or black. Lean green, blue and chartreuse for anything deep.

citations.quote: visible light of long wavelengths (e.g. red, orange) is absorbed more in water than light of shorter wavelengths (green, blue).

provenance.basis: editorial rule, grounded in the cited fish-vision science; to be calibrated by the logbook

principles.label: Deep water goes blue-green
principles.rule: Below the thermocline only blue/green light persists, so a bait that looks natural on the surface can go flat down deep — contrast and profile do the work.

citations.quote: Shorter wavelengths penetrate further, with blue and green light reaching the deepest depths.
Blue is the only colour of light available at depth underwater, so it is the only colour that can be reflected back to the eye, and everything has a blue tinge under water.

provenance.basis: editorial rule, grounded in the cited fish-vision science; to be calibrated by the logbook

principles.label: True colors only near the surface
principles.rule: Natural, translucent colors read true only in the top few feet — that's where color-matching forage pays off.

citations.quote: Objects in water will only appear as their real colours near the surface where all wavelengths of light are still available

provenance.basis: editorial rule, grounded in the cited fish-vision science; to be calibrated by the logbook

principles.label: Contrast beats color
principles.rule: In low light or stained water, choose baits that contrast with the background (dark/black, chartreuse, black-and-blue) rather than natural shades.

citations.quote: The study indicates that an object's contrast against the background, rather than colour, may be more important for object detection.

provenance.basis: editorial rule, grounded in the cited fish-vision science; to be calibrated by the logbook

principles.label: Low light runs on rods
principles.rule: At night and deep dusk, color vision is out — go dark silhouette, big profile, and vibration over color.

citations.quote: The fish retina has rod cells that provide high visual sensitivity in low light conditions and cone cells that provide higher temporal and spatial resolution than the rod cells are capable of.

provenance.basis: editorial rule, grounded in the cited fish-vision science; to be calibrated by the logbook

principles.label: Clear water rewards color
principles.rule: In clear water with good light, fish have the wavelengths — and the cones — to see color; natural forage matching is strongest there.

citations.quote: Colour vision is more useful in environments with a broader range of wavelengths available, e.g., near the surface in clear waters rather than in deeper water where only a narrow band of wavelengths persist.

provenance.basis: editorial rule, grounded in the cited fish-vision science; to be calibrated by the logbook
